schools.summary: Henry: a boy of eight, whose infancy did not bar his right; the reform waited till his twelfth year, but 'those that seek God early shall find him.'
Keil sets the Chronicle beside Kings — more exact, more complete, events kept in time-order; Ellicott adds the mother's name Jedidah of Boscath from 2 Kings 22:1.
Gill fixes the bare datum of the eight-year-old king and refers the rest to the parallel.
Clarke lays out the whole roadmap of the chapter — purge, repair, the found book, Huldah, the covenant.

themes: the last light before the dark

schools.summary: Gill: seeking God = prayer and the knowledge of his will and worship; records Kimchi, Jarchi, and the Targum on the young king's seeking.
Wesley: at sixteen, entering the age of temptation and with none to restrain him, he begins to be religious in good earnest.
Ellicott: the dates are peculiar to the Chronicler; the purging was begun not finished in the twelfth year (v.33), and he rejects Thenius's and Noldeke's suspicions of the arrangement.

themes: the eighth year and the twelfth

schools.summary: Gill: the king went in person to see the altars of Manasseh, rebuilt by Amon, broken down.

Ellicott identifies the sun-statues and sacred pillars and the dust 'sprinkled on the graves' as though they were guilty; Keil reads the strewn dust and burnt bones as one act of defilement summarising 2 Kings 23.
Clarke: the religion of a land is as the religion of its king — 'the people were as one man with the king.'

themes: a nation's worship follows its throne

schools.summary: Gill hears the fulfilment of the man of God's prophecy at Bethel (1 Kings 13:2), spoken above 350 years before, that Josiah would burn the priests' bones on the altar.

Keil and Ellicott describe the deliberate, irreparable defilement — bones taken from the graves and burnt on the altars — with Ellicott noting the horror of such violation (Amos 2:1) and the Chronicler's added 'cleansed.'
Clarke fixes the kemarim of the Targum, the idolatrous priests, pointing to 2 Kings 23:5.

Ellicott and Keil explain how a ruined, deported north lay open to Josiah, and reckon Simeon among the northern tribes (its Beersheba a pilgrimage sanctuary); both wrestle with the obscure word rendered 'mattocks.'
Wesley: Naphtali the utmost border, the ten tribes gone, the newcomers too weak to resist; Clarke: spade and axe finished the reformation.
Gill: the remnant of the northern tribes, after the Assyrian captivity, had become subject to the kings of Judah.

debates.question: What does the obscure word the AV renders 'with their mattocks' mean?

sides.position: 'in their ruins' — qualifying the cities the Assyrians had laid waste
the received text yields no sense; the marginal reading is 'with their swords'

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the 'idols' as sun-statues absent from the parallel; Keil reads 'returned to Jerusalem' as the hinge, the purging of land and house being the ground on which the temple-repair now proceeds.
Gill glosses the altars and groves of the statues and images in them.

themes: from tearing down to building up

schools.summary: Henry makes the repair a lesson on cleansing then renewing the temple of the heart, and on the fellowship of varied gifts — hands and heads, burden-bearers and overseers, each needing the other.
Gill dates it to the king's twenty-sixth year, the purging six years in the doing.
Wesley: 'the house' is the house of God, so called by way of eminence.
Keil and Ellicott trace the flow of the funds (as under Joash, 2 Chron 24:11) and read the last clause as 'the inhabitants of Jerusalem,' not 'they returned'; the enumeration of givers is rhetorical.
Clarke argues 'they returned to Jerusalem' should be 'the inhabitants of Jerusalem,' supported by MSS and all the versions (cf. 2 Chron 19:8).
Gill: the commissioners came to consult Hilkiah about the repair.
Ellicott: 'the workmen' are the overseers or contractors (2 Chron 24:12), the rare verb 'to repair' occurring here only; Keil sets the two-stage handling beside the Joash repair.
Gill: the king's ministers put the money into the workmen's hands.
Ellicott: hewn stone, timber for couplings, and the raftering of the chambers 'the kings of Judah had destroyed' (cf. Athaliah's sons, 2 Chron 24:7; Ahaz, 2 Chron 28:24).
Gill: the artificers and builders are the masons and carpenters.
Wesley: 'the houses' are the chambers joining the temple.

themes: the chambers the kings had ruined
the temple scarred by its own kings

schools.summary: Ellicott: the men worked 'in good faith,' so no reckoning of the money was required (2 Kings 22:7); the overseers' names and musical offices are the Chronicler's own touch.
Gill: the labourers and their inspectors did the work faithfully.
Wesley: the Levite musicians were exercised in both work and worship; Clarke conjectures they played to cheer the workmen.

outliers.note: An antiquarian excursus: the fable of Amphion's harp raising the walls of Thebes preserves, on the testimony of a recovered Greek treatise on music, the memory of a harper who played to lighten the labourers' toil — so perhaps the Levite musicians played to the temple workmen.

themes: labour to the sound of praise

schools.summary: Ellicott: the musical guilds of Levites, set over the burden-bearers, probably cheered the labour with song (as in ancient Egypt), and furnished scribes, officers, and porters (1 Chron 23:4-5; 2:55).
Gill: the foremen kept the burden-bearers diligent so the workmen never stood idle for want of materials.

themes: the dignity of the musical guilds

schools.summary: Keil: the book is 'given by the hand of Moses,' not necessarily his autograph; Ellicott supplies the traditions of the finding (Josephus, the Rabbinic hiding from Ahaz) and that this verse is the Chronicler's supplement, not in Kings.
Henry turns to thanksgiving that Bibles are now 'in all hands' — jewels, but not rarities — and warns against accounting the common word a strange thing.
Gill traces the finding to the bringing-out of the temple money.
Clarke refers the reader to the fuller notice at 2 Kings 22:8.

themes: the book of the law found
the wonder of Bibles in every hand

schools.summary: Henry: the people were well taught, well fixed, and well tended, yet all Josiah's days were days of restraint on hearts still leaning to idols — a reformation baffled by a hypocritical return (Jer 3:6; Ezek 4:6).
Gill refers the account of the reading and the covenant to the parallel in 2 Kings 23.

Ellicott: the summary glances back to the northern purge (v.6); 'made to serve, even to serve' is unique to the Chronicler, but 'all his days they departed not' betrays a merely outward conformity, undone by the relapse after Josiah's death.
Gill: Josiah took away all the abominations out of every country of the children of Israel.
Wesley: the repeated 'even to serve' shows this was the one thing the king's heart was set upon — to engage the people to God and their duty.

Ellicott: the encomium 'neither right nor left' is pronounced of no other king, equivalent to a perfect keeping of the law of the king (Deut 17:20); Keil binds the verdict to the seeking and purging that follow.
Clarke reads the golden mean — a steady hand, zeal without excess and caution without cowardice; 'let this pious youth be thy exemplar.'

Keil records Hilkiah's announcement — 'I have found the book' — and its delivery to Shaphan, setting the verse at the head of the movement (discovery, dismay, Huldah) that runs parallel to 2 Kings 22:8-10.

themes: a recovery, not a mere discovery
the book takes over the reform

schools.summary: Keil sets out the weighty embassy — Hilkiah, Ahikam, Abdon, Shaphan, Asaiah — sent to 'inquire of the LORD,' running parallel throughout to 2 Kings 22:12.

Keil sets out the whole assembly, great and small, and the king reading the book of the covenant; Ellicott marks the Chronicler's 'Levites' for the 'prophets' of Kings, the prophetic order being extinct in his day.
Clarke refers the going-up to the parallel at 2 Kings 23:1.

themes: the whole people in the temple
the recovered word before all hearts

schools.summary: Ellicott restores the defective 'they that the king had appointed' from the versions, traces the variants in Huldah's genealogy (Tikvath, Hasrah), and locates her 'in the college' — the lower city.
Clarke identifies Huldah the prophetess and refers to the fuller note at 2 Kings 22:14.
Clarke draws from the Targum the distinction between the meymera, the personal Word before whom Josiah humbled himself, and the pithgam, the words spoken — a hint of the Word who is a Person.
Henry: humble yourself and seek God as Josiah did; though it cannot turn wrath from the land, it delivers your own soul — the tenderness that could not save the kingdom saved the king.

themes: God looks on the melted heart

schools.summary: Clarke refers to the fuller note on 'gathered to thy grave in peace' at 2 Kings 22:20.
Henry: death made the matter of a promise — welcomed, like Noah housed in the ark before the deluge, as a gathering-in before the evil comes.

themes: gathered to the grave in peace
peace from the ruin, not the sword
the mercy of an early grave

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'in his place' is 'on his stand' — the same royal station as at Joash's crowning (2 Chron 23:13) — and 'a covenant' is properly 'the covenant' of the law just read.
Clarke refers to the parallel at 2 Kings 23:3 and to the preceding chapter for the circumstances.
Clarke: the people rose to their feet to testify their assent; Wesley: they engaged by oath to keep laws they already owed, no new duty but a fresh binding.
Ellicott: 'he caused to stand' and 'the people stood' differ only in unwritten vowels; 'and Benjamin' is likely a corruption of 'into the covenant'; the kept covenant is the Chronicler's addition.

themes: the people bound to the covenant
an oath to a duty already owed
the covenant kept in the doing

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'brought the book in' is only a re-pointing of 'the scribe came in' (2 Kings 22:9), the rest the Chronicler's addition; Keil finds no difference of fact between the accounts, the Chronicler only naming the book outright.
Ellicott: 'gathered together' is 'poured out' from the chest, the overseers and workmen being one body (2 Kings 22:9); Keil sets the notice within Shaphan's faithful back-report to the king.

Ellicott: the verse is all but identical with 2 Kings 22:10, 'read in it' for 'read it,' and refuses to make the change imply a large book; Keil takes the reading as the culmination of the book's passage to the king.

themes: the book read before the king

schools.summary: Ellicott: the Chronicler enlarges 'the people' to 'them that are left in Israel and Judah' (the northern remnant) and writes wrath 'poured out' for 'kindled,' remembering the ruin of the ten tribes.
Henry: under conviction we are directed to inquire of the Lord, as Josiah did — 'what shall we do?', 'what must I do to be saved?'

themes: the remnant of Israel and Judah

schools.summary: Ellicott: 'I am about to bring' (participle), the doom at the door; 'all the curses written in the book' is the Chronicler's paraphrase, pointing to the Deuteronomic sanctions (Deut 28; 29; Joshua 8:34).
Henry: a standing warning of the ruin sin brings on nations — those who forsake God kindle a fire that shall not be quenched.

themes: all the curses of the book
too late to turn the wrath

schools.summary: Ellicott: the plural 'works,' the 'poured out' for 'kindled' (though 'kindled' fits 'not quenched' better), and the causative form of 'burned incense' — the Chronicler's characteristic retelling.
Henry reads it with v.24 as one warning: forsaking God kindles an unquenchable fire, the sober end of a people that persists in provoking him.

themes: wrath poured out and not quenched

schools.summary: Ellicott follows the pivot to the king in the grammar — 'through the LORD,' the added 'humbledst thyself,' the shorter 'weep,' the emphatic 'I,' the plural 'graves,' the added 'inhabitants' — the Chronicler retelling the oracle in his own idiom.

themes: the pivot from wrath to mercy
doom for the place, mercy for the penitent

schools.summary: Wesley: were scripture as new to us as to Josiah, it would strike deeper; it is not less weighty for being well known.
Henry: God was well pleased with the rent garments, but 'rend the heart, and not the garments' — the outward sign nothing without the inward grief.
Keil names it the king's dismay at the book, which drives him to inquire of Huldah (parallel 2 Kings 22:11-20).
